summary: Nahʔą Dehé, the South Nahanni River, runs through the Mackenzie Mountains of the south-western Northwest Territories, plunging over Náįlįcho (Virginia Falls) and through four deep canyons. There are no roads: visitors fly in by floatplane, for a day at the falls or for a river trip of one to three weeks. Climbers come for the granite walls of the Cirque of the Unclimbables. A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1978.

facts.suggestedTime: A day by floatplane, or one to three weeks on the river

story: Three events made this country. For hundreds of millions of years seas covered it and laid down up to 6,000 metres of sandstone, shale, limestone and dolomite. From about 200 million years ago the drift of the continents folded and lifted those layers, and around 110 million years ago molten rock rose beneath them and cooled into the granite that now stands bare in the Ragged Range. Then came ice, though the last glaciation, which ended 10,000 years ago, reached only the far east and west of the park. The river held its course as the mountains rose, cutting the deepest canyons in Canada.

The South Nahanni rises outside the park in the Selwyn Mountains and flows 563 kilometres to the Liard River below Nahanni Butte. At Náįlįcho it drops more than 90 metres in a single curtain split by a rock stack, then enters Fourth, Third, Second and First canyons. Hot springs warmed by the same deep heat that raised the granite surface along the way: at Gahnįhthah, Rabbitkettle, the water has built the largest tufa mounds in Canada, terraces of calcium carbonate that the Dene hold sacred as the home of Yamba Deja, the horizon walker who created Dene law.

The park reaches from lowland to alpine tundra, and its plant life is richer than anywhere of comparable size in the continental Northwest Territories: more than 700 species of vascular plants, among them the Nahanni aster, known nowhere else. Forty-two mammal species have been recorded, including grizzly and black bears, wolves, moose, woodland caribou, Dall's sheep and mountain goats, and 180 species of bird; trumpeter swans nest on Yohin Lake, and up to four species of loon can be found on Rabbitkettle Lake.

Dene people and their ancestors have used this land for up to 10,000 years. In the late nineteenth century Mountain Dene families floated down the river each spring in boats of six to ten moose hides stretched over spruce frames, up to 20 metres long, to trade their furs at the posts. The park reserve was established in 1976, became one of the first World Heritage Sites in 1978, and was expanded in 2009, with the support of the Dehcho First Nations and Nahʔą Dehé Dene Band, to about 30,050 square kilometres. It remains a reserve pending the settlement of Indigenous land claims, and it is managed together with the Dehcho First Nations and Nahʔą Dehé Dene Band.
howItWorks: Nahanni is a national park reserve, set aside under the Canada National Parks Act until Indigenous land claims in the region are settled, and run by Parks Canada with the Dehcho First Nations and Nahʔą Dehé Dene Band. Indigenous people may hunt, trap, fish and harvest in the park and use motorised transport to do so; no one else may operate a motor boat, all-terrain vehicle, snowmobile or any other motor vehicle, or fire a gun. There are no public roads. Almost everyone arrives by chartered floatplane, from Fort Simpson, Yellowknife, Muncho Lake in British Columbia or Watson Lake in Yukon, and aircraft may land only at the designated sites — Náįlįcho (Virginia Falls), Glacier Lake, Bunny Bar, Island Lakes, Honeymoon Lake, Seaplane Lake and Gahnįhthah Mįe (Rabbitkettle Lake) — or elsewhere with a permit. Use a charter company with a valid national park business licence.

Day visitors may land only at Náįlįcho and Glacier Lake. Every visitor, day or overnight, pays the park user fee, either to the park office or on arrival at Náįlįcho. Every overnight trip, in Nahanni and in neighbouring Nááts'įhch'oh, must be reserved in advance and registered: groups are limited to 12, and the reservation is confirmed only once each member has paid the Northern Park Backcountry Excursion Fee by phone to the Fort Simpson office. Register in person, by phone or by email within 24 hours of entering the park, when staff will give you current closures, recent bear activity, fires and fire bans; de-register within 24 hours of the date on your form. Guided groups have the bookings made by their outfitter.

Náįlįcho is the pinch point. Only 24 people a day — 12 travelling privately and 12 with commercial outfitters — may arrive there, camping on the narrow portage is limited to two nights, and peak season runs from 1 July to 15 August, so book early and give an alternative date. Camping is also limited, and reserved, at Rabbitkettle Lake, Glacier Lake and Fairy Meadows, and at Nááts'įhch'oh Tué (Moose Ponds) and Ǫtaa Tué Fehto (Divide Lake) upstream. Parks Canada staff are at Náįlįcho and Rabbitkettle Lake through the summer, and a warden is on call around the clock from 15 June to 15 September. Black and grizzly bears are common, and areas — most often around Rabbitkettle Lake — are closed whenever grizzlies are about; the tufa mounds can be visited only on a hike guided by park staff. Fires are allowed only in a fire box or fire pan, or in fireplaces at designated campgrounds.

sights.name: Náįlįcho (Virginia Falls)
sights.note: The South Nahanni plunges more than 90 metres around a central rock stack. Day flights land here; interpreters lead a walk to a viewpoint above the Sluicebox Rapids.

sights.name: Cirque of the Unclimbables
sights.note: Granite walls and spires in the Ragged Range, among them the Lotus Flower Tower. Reached by floatplane to Glacier Lake and a strenuous six-kilometre, unmaintained route to Fairy Meadows.

sights.name: Glacier Lake
sights.note: One of only two day-use landing sites, below the Ragged Range, with food caches for climbers bound for the Cirque.

sights.name: Gahnįhthah (Rabbitkettle Hotsprings tufa mounds)
sights.note: Canada's largest tufa mounds, terraces built by 20 °C spring water. A special preservation area, seen only on hikes led by park staff.

sights.name: Gahnįhthah Mįe (Rabbitkettle Lake)
sights.note: A staffed summer landing site and the start of many river trips, two to three days' paddling above Náįlįcho. Up to four species of loon and red-necked grebes can be seen here.

sights.name: The Gate and Pulpit Rock
sights.note: In Third Canyon the river turns a hairpin through a narrow gap beside a 460-metre limestone wall, with the pinnacle of Pulpit Rock on the east side.

sights.name: Deadmen Valley
sights.note: A calm stretch between Second and First canyons below the Tlogotsho Plateau. Its mineral licks draw Dall's sheep; stopping at the licks is prohibited.

sights.name: First Canyon
sights.note: The last and highest of the four canyons, cut through resistant limestone, with the park's highest vertical walls.

sights.name: Kraus Hotsprings
sights.note: Two sulphurous springs at the foot of First Canyon, named after Mary and Gus Kraus, who lived here from 1940 to 1971. Camping closes from 1 August.

sights.name: Nahanni Parks Canada Office, Fort Simpson
sights.note: The park's main office in Łįįdłįį Kų́e (Fort Simpson): reservations, registration and fee payment. Open daily in July and August.

entrances: By chartered floatplane from Łįįdłįį Kų́e (Fort Simpson), Yellowknife, Muncho Lake (British Columbia) or Watson Lake (Yukon) to a designated landing site
Day flights to Náįlįcho (Virginia Falls) and Glacier Lake, the only day-use sites

River trips starting at Náįlįcho (7 to 10 days), Gahnįhthah Mįe (Rabbitkettle Lake, 10 to 14 days), Island Lakes (14 to 18 days) or, in Nááts'įhch'oh, the Moose Ponds and Divide Lake (about three weeks)
Overland by the unmaintained road from Watson Lake to Tungsten, often impassable and four-wheel drive only, then down the Little Nahanni or Flat rivers — Class IV and V rapids, for experts only
planYourVisit.reservations: Every overnight trip must be reserved in advance with the Reservation Request Form, emailed to the park office, and each group member must pay the Northern Park Backcountry Excursion Fee before the reservation is confirmed. Reservations are first come, first served; peak season is 1 July to 15 August, and Náįlįcho takes only 24 arrivals a day. Cancel before 31 March for a 50 per cent refund; after that the fee cannot be refunded but can be deferred to the next year. Check with the park office before you go.
permits: Trip reservation and registration for every overnight trip, and de-registration within 24 hours of leaving
Nahanni fishing permit, under the National Parks of Canada Fishing Regulations
Permit to land an aircraft anywhere but the designated sites; request it at least 90 days ahead
Custodial permit for youth groups, and permits for research, commercial filming and photography, food or fuel caches, and travel on the Howard's Pass Access Road
camping: Náįlįcho: a maximum of two nights, by reservation
Reserved camping at Gahnįhthah Mįe (Rabbitkettle Lake) and Glacier Lake/Fairy Meadows, with rustic, unmaintained facilities
Elevated food caches at the designated campgrounds — Rabbitkettle Lake, Náįlįcho and Kraus Hotsprings — must be used for all food and garbage
No camping at Kraus Hotsprings from 1 August or at Whitespray; no overnight stay at Pulpit Rock/the Gate or Lafferty Creek without the means to pack out human waste
lodging: None in the park; accommodation in Fort Simpson and the other gateway communities
seasonalClosures: Areas, most often around Rabbitkettle Lake, close whenever grizzly bears are present — check with the park office before you go
Camping at Kraus Hotsprings closes on 1 August each year
The Nahanni Butte office is closed from October to June

weather: The climate is cold continental, and the mountains make it changeable. At the start of the season in June temperatures range from below freezing to 25 °C; July and August are the warmest months, from 0 °C to 30 °C, with showers and thunderstorms building in the late afternoon and the most severe storms in July. Snow can fall in any month. By late August there can be frost at night, September often freezes, and ice begins to form on the river in early October. The river peaks in early to mid-June with snowmelt and is usually steadiest in August. Low cloud can stop flights at any time.
directions: There are no roads into the park. The main gateway is Łįįdłįį Kų́e (Fort Simpson), where the park office is; floatplanes also fly from Yellowknife, Muncho Lake in British Columbia and Watson Lake in Yukon. Day flights land at Náįlįcho or Glacier Lake; river parties are dropped at a designated landing site, and many paddle all the way to Nahanni Butte, the Dene community about a mile up the South Nahanni from its meeting with the Liard, where Parks Canada keeps a second office. Booking a flight does not replace the park reservation.

fees.title: Northern Park Backcountry excursion/camping
fees.detail: Paid by all day and overnight visitors, at the park office or on arrival at Náįlįcho; overnight visitors must pay before their reservation is confirmed. CA$259.00 for an annual pass, valid at Aulavik, Auyuittuq, Ivvavik, Nahanni, Nááts'įhch'oh, Quttinirpaaq, Sirmilik, Tuktut Nogait, Vuntut, Qausuittuq and Ukkusiksalik. Youth 17 and under are free. As listed by Parks Canada in November 2026.

fees.title: Fishing permit
fees.detail: CA$51.25 for an annual permit. As listed by Parks Canada in November 2026.

chronology.text: Dene people and their ancestors begin using the lands in and around the park.
Mountain Dene families travel down the river each spring in mooseskin boats to trade furs at the posts.
Nahanni National Park Reserve is established, covering 4,766 square kilometres.
The park reserve is inscribed as one of the first UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
The South Nahanni within the park is designated a Canadian Heritage River.
A landslide dam on Clearwater Creek partly collapses, raising the river in Deadmen Valley by more than four metres overnight.
The Interim Park Management Arrangement with the Dehcho First Nations sets up the Nahʔą Dehé Consensus Team.
The park reserve is expanded to about 30,050 square kilometres, taking in the Ram Plateau and the North Nahanni Karst.
Canada, the Nahʔą Dehé Dene Band and the Dehcho First Nations sign the Ndahecho Gondié Gháádé shared-governance agreement in September.

safety: The river is cold, usually 5 to 10 °C in summer, and a capsize brings on hypothermia fast. Wear a wet suit or dry suit for whitewater, and know the river's rapids before you run them.

Rain can raise the river and its side creeks suddenly. Steep, narrow valleys such as Dry Canyon Creek, Prairie Creek and Lafferty Creek can flash-flood; one hiker died in Dry Canyon Creek in 1995. Never camp low by tributary mouths, and avoid the Clearwater Creek delta.

Black and grizzly bears live throughout the park. Store all food and garbage in the caches where they are provided, keep a clean camp, and obey area closures. Bear spray cannot be brought across the border; buy it in Canada and check with your airline.
The Cirque hike is an unmaintained, strenuous route over steep, overgrown ground. Help is far away and weather can ground aircraft for days.
regulations: Recreational drones are prohibited; flying one can bring a fine of up to $25,000.

Eight special preservation areas — the Rabbitkettle tufa mounds, Wildmint and Old Pots hot springs, Grotte Valerie, Yohin Lake, the Sand Blowouts, the Deadmen Valley sheep licks and the poljes — are closed without a permit, and no one may enter a cave.
Fires only in a fire box or fire pan, or in fireplaces at designated campgrounds; burn only dead wood from the ground.
Pack out all garbage. Do not feed or touch wildlife, or remove plants, antlers, fossils, rocks or cultural objects.
Firearms must be unloaded and cased in transit; only Indigenous harvesters may hunt or use motorised transport.
